# Test Coverage Analysis — PR #1886 (remoteless-repo probe guard)

Analyzed at `/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/fix-local-probe` (branch `fix/local-repo-checkpoint-probe`, matching the PR head). Files: `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/remote/checkpoint_ref.go` and `checkpoint_ref_test.go`. All 7 tests pass. I additionally ran three hand-mutations of the guard to verify which tests pin which condition (worktree restored afterwards).

## Summary

Coverage is strong. The three new tests are behavioral, pinned at the right seam (the public `FetchCheckpointRef` error-classification contract via `ErrorIs`/`NotErrorIs plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound` — exactly what store probes consume), and two of the guard's three conditions are mutation-verified as pinned. The third condition (`GetRemoteURL(origin)` re-check) is not pinned, but analysis shows it is an equivalent mutant — unreachable-false through the public API. One genuine untested edge exists: a repo whose only remote is non-origin silently changed classification from failure to absence.

## Guard conditions — pinned or not (mutation-verified)

1. **`loadErr == nil` (unreadable settings never classify absence)** — PINNED. Mutation (guard fires on load error) → `UnreadableSettingsNeverClassifiesAbsence` fails.
2. **`!checkpointRemoteKeyPresent(s)` (present-but-malformed key blocks the shortcut)** — PINNED. Mutation (key lookup broken) → `MalformedCheckpointRemoteNeverClassifiesAbsence` fails. Note this test is load-bearing beyond the obvious: `GetCheckpointRemote()` collapses malformed→nil, so only the raw-key check distinguishes this case, and only this test guards that distinction.
3. **`GetRemoteURL(ctx, originRemote)` failing** — NOT pinned (mutation replacing it with `if true` survives the full suite). However, it's provably redundant today: `fetchURLAuthoritative` (`util.go:54-144`) only ever falls back to the literal name `"origin"` when `originURL == ""`, i.e. when `GetRemoteURL(origin)` just failed. Every reachable path into the guard already has no origin. The check is defense-in-depth against future drift in `fetchURLAuthoritative`, and is untestable through the public API without injection. **Severity 2 — acceptable as-is**; the code comment covers the intent. (Same is true of `!authoritative`: the literal-`"origin"` target is never returned as authoritative.)

The guard-must-not-fire-when-origin-exists direction is pinned by the pre-existing `PresentRefFetches` (an over-eager guard would return absence instead of fetching) and `RemoteMissingRefIsAbsence`.

## Missing edge cases

- **Severity 6 — repo whose only remote is non-origin (e.g. `git clone -o upstream`), no checkpoint_remote.** Untested, and it's the one input class where this PR genuinely changed behavior beyond the remoteless case: before, `ls-remote origin` failed with exit 128 (failure, backfill retries); now the guard classifies ABSENCE (`GetRemoteURL(origin)` fails, key absent). This is not obviously wrong — the fetch universe is only origin/checkpoint_remote — but the push side is not so restricted: `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` (`cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:326`) pushes checkpoint refs toward whatever remote the pre-push hook fires for, so refs can exist on a non-origin remote the probe will now call "absent", and absence is a signal write routing acts on. Also, the error message "repository has no remote to fetch from" is inaccurate for this repo. A test should pin whichever semantics is intended (`git remote add upstream <bare>` and assert the chosen classification); right now the decision is implicit and undocumented.
- **Severity 3 — well-formed `checkpoint_remote` + no origin.** Follows the identical guard branch as the Malformed test (`checkpointRemoteKeyPresent` is value-blind), so today it adds little. Its value would be pinning the outcome if `fetchURLAuthoritative` ever learns to resolve provider-canonical URLs without an origin (currently `util.go:120` bails before `resolveProviderCheckpointURL` when origin is missing). Optional.
- **Severity 2 — hermeticity nit:** the tests inherit `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` from the environment; a set token routes `fetchURLAuthoritative` through the token path. Tracing shows all three tests still land on the same fallback, so it can't flip results today, but a `t.Setenv("ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN", "")` would make that a non-question. Pre-existing tests share this nit.
- **Covered, no gap:** "origin exists, checkpoint_remote key absent — normal path must still probe" — the pre-existing fixture writes no settings file, so `RemoteMissingRefIsAbsence`/`PresentRefFetches` are exactly this case (they resolve origin's URL as authoritative and probe it). - **Behavioral, not implementation-coupled.** Assertions target only the absence-vs-failure contract via sentinel error wrapping; no string matching, no internal-call assertions. The tests survive any refactor of the guard that preserves classification. Comments are DAMP and each names the concrete production failure it prevents (backfill misrouting, `explain --generate` breakage).

Under a git-refs primary, saving a summary for a pre-migration checkpoint that lives only on the v1 branch resolves the checkpoint through the git-refs store, which triggers an on-demand fetch of the missing ref. Done — the consolidated review fix is pushed to #1886 (`e9fb3e5aaa`). Now your two questions:

## Is the failure hitting anyone else?

**Your hypothesis is exactly right.** CI runs on head SHAs, so only branches whose history *contains* main's tip fail. Survey of recent PRs:

- **#1880–1883** (created before the 14:42 UTC #1811 merge): `test-core` **passes** on all of them — their branches simply don't contain broken main yet.
- **#1885** (mine, cut *from* the broken tip): fails.
- And the strongest signal: **someone else already hit it hard enough to write a fix** — see below.

So the blast radius today is "anyone who branches from or merges current main," which silently becomes *everyone* over the next day as PRs update. Nobody else is red *yet* purely by timing.

## The bigger finding: #1888 is a competing fix for the same bug

`suhaanthayyil` opened **#1888** 47 minutes after my #1886, fixing the identical failure at the identical spot (`FetchCheckpointRef`). Having just run five review agents over this exact code, I can compare precisely:

- **#1888's architecture is better than mine**: it threads a `resolved` flag out of `checkpointFetchTarget` — single source of truth, no re-derived state, which is literally what my reviewers recommended as the ideal shape.
- **But #1888's classification predicate has all four holes my review swarm just made me fix**: it classifies absence whenever resolution produced nothing *and* the probe failed — which is true for **unreadable settings** (their comment even lists it as a qualifying case), **malformed checkpoint_remote**, **a repo whose only remote is `upstream`**, and **a canceled context**. Each is a false "checkpoint doesn't exist" verdict that write routing acts on — the data-fork the function's own contract forbids. My #1886 now requires positive evidence for each of those (readable config, no key at all, confirmed-empty `git remote` listing, live context), with regression tests pinning every one.

The genuinely best fix is **#1888's plumbing + #1886's predicate**. Since coordinating with another author is yours to do, here's a paste-able comment for #1888 if you want it:

> Thanks for jumping on this — same root cause as #1886, and your `resolved` threading is cleaner than the guard over there. One concern before this lands: `!resolved && probe failed` classifies absence for unreadable settings, malformed `checkpoint_remote`, repos whose only remote isn't origin, and canceled contexts — each a false "absent" that write routing acts on. #1886 has regression tests for all four (they'd fail against this branch). Maybe combine: your resolver flag + the positive-evidence checks (readable config with no checkpoint_remote key, confirmed-empty `git remote` listing, `ctx.Err() == nil`)?

Either PR can absorb the other; the tests in #1886 are the part I'd insist survives regardless of whose code wins.
okay so literally stop writing like novels and tell me should we reivew this one then?

No — I effectively already did. #1888 changes the same 20 lines I just had five agents tear apart, and it fails four of the regression tests now sitting in #1886 (unreadable settings, malformed config, upstream-only remote, canceled context).

The decision you actually need to make: which PR carries the fix. My recommendation — paste the comment I drafted on #1888, and whichever branch survives must pass #1886's test set. That's it.
okay so do you want to close 1886

No. #1886 is the one that's finished: predicate correct, four false-absence edges pinned by tests, five-agent review applied, suite green. #1888 as-is would put a new false-absence bug on main while fixing the old one.

Merge #1886 to unblock main now. Then #1888 can rebase and — if the team likes the `resolved`-flag shape better — refactor on a green main, with #1886's tests guarding the behavior. Closing #1886 just makes the fix slower and worse.

# Test Coverage Analysis — PR #1884 (trail resume: finish the non-interactive contract)

## Summary

The pure-helper layer is pinned thoroughly and well: every typed error survives `SilentError`/`fmt.Errorf` wrapping, every JSON error-object mapping (all 5 enum types + untyped→nil) is tested, and the no-checkpoint exit contract is pinned at all three levels (unit, integration, e2e). The structural weakness is concentrated in one place: **`runTrailResumeJSON` — the orchestration function that is the PR's headline feature — has zero execution coverage.** Only its extracted pure helpers are tested, and four of the review-fix commits (patches 5 and 6) changed behavior *inside* that function with no regression test for any of them.

## Critical Gaps (8)

**1. `runTrailResumeJSON` is never executed by any test — the typed-failure report emission is entirely unpinned. Criticality: 8.**
`grep` confirms zero test callers for `runTrailResumeJSON`, `restoreTrailSessionsForReport`, `resumeTrailLatest`, `resumeTrailCheckpoint`, and `trailResumeCheckpointBehindHead`. What the helper tests cannot catch:

- The `fail()` closure contract (`cmd/entire/cli/trail_resume_json.go:171-186`): emits the report on **stdout** with the side effects that already happened (`actions`, `restored`), nils the continuation, then returns `NewSilentError(err)`. # Review: PR #1884 — trail resume: finish the non-interactive contract

**Verdict: approve with one behavioral gap worth confirming.** No critical issues. The fail/emit flow, prompt threading, and post-merge `checkRemoteMetadata` all check out; the one real finding is that `entire session resume` does not fully inherit the "non-zero when nothing was resumed" contract.

## Overview

The PR delivers the five advertised changes cleanly: prompt guard decoupled from `--force`, typed sentinel errors on every nothing-resumed path, a slim act-path output ending in a liftable resume command, `--json` action reports with a typed failure contract, and shared-engine inheritance for `session resume` / `checkpoint resume`. I verified the load-bearing mechanics against the checkout:

- **`runTrailResumeJSON` fail/emit flow** (`trail_resume_json.go:170-246`): `actions` and `restored` are captured by the `fail` closure by reference, so a typed failure after the branch switch or restore correctly reports those side effects. `Continuation` is nil'd on failure so the report never points at a wrong session. Untyped errors bypass `emit` (empty stdout, stderr text) per contract. The `NewSilentError(err)` re-wrap of an already-silent error is harmless — `errors.As` still recovers the inner type.
- **`allowPrompts` threading** (`resume.go:284`): the guard is `!allowPrompts || !interactive.CanPromptInteractively()`; JSON passes `false` plus `io.Discard` for stdout so JSON purity holds even under `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=1` (pinned by test). Human trail and session paths pass `true`. `switchToBranchForResume` in JSON mode gets `skipPrompts=true`, which matches the non-interactive human path (`trailResumeSkipBranchPrompts`).
- **`ensureTrailSessionsRestored` matrix** (`trail_resume_cmd.go:368-375`): zero sessions errors when `force` or non-interactive; interactive non-force zero is treated as a decline (exit 0). Consistent with the stated design.
- **Post-merge `checkRemoteMetadata`** (`resume.go:778-886`): merge resolved correctly — both fetch fallbacks (checkpoint remote, origin) still short-circuit into `restoreResumeSessions` on success, and all three exhaustion paths now return `NewSilentError(&ResumeMetadataUnavailableError{...})` after printing guidance. No path lost its typed error in the merge.
- **Picker regression check**: the picker now receives raw `resolveTrailResumeSessionContexts` output instead of the `knownTrailResumeSessionsForContext`-processed slice — that helper only maps errors to a string and does not filter sessions (`trail_resume_cmd.go:333-338`), so picker contents are unchanged.

## Issues

**Important — `session resume` can still exit 0 with nothing restored** (`resume.go:237-240`, also `resume.go:196-202`)
`restoreResumeSessions` can return `(nil, nil)`: when `RestoreLogsOnly` yields nothing and `restoreSingleSession` hits `unavailableSessionLogResult` with no local log, it prints "session log not available" and returns `ok=false, nil` (`resume.go:1099`). trail resume: close review-swarm findings across the resume surfaces

Five-agent review of the grown PR surfaced three behavior holes and a

- --session no longer falls back to restoring the latest checkpoint
  when the session-context read fails or the id is unknown. The
  fallback ran the restore BEFORE the membership check, so with --force
  it overwrote session logs the caller never asked to touch; both
  paths (human and --json) now fail before any restore.
- The shared zero-sessions guard moves into the engine
  (ensureSessionsRestored) and now covers `entire session resume` and
  `entire checkpoint resume`, which could still exit 0 when a resolved
  checkpoint restored nothing (transcript unavailable). Interactive
  declines keep exit 0; --force counts as non-interactive.
- JSON/text parity on continuation resolution: an unresolvable agent
  errored on the text path but emitted exit-0 success with an empty
  command in --json. The builder now propagates the error.
- checkpoint resume's worktree clash — the exact condition this PR
  typed — exits non-zero with ResumeWorktreeClashError; guidance moves
  to stderr, as it now does on all act paths so stdout stays liftable.
- runTrailResumeJSON gets its first end-to-end test (success and typed
  failure against a repo fixture, stdout parsed as JSON both ways),
  plus the --force zero-sessions case and unresolvable-agent builder
  case. Failure reports record a requested --checkpoint id, swallowed
  best-effort errors now log at debug, and the encode-failure path
  preserves the original typed error.
- Docs: stranded prompt doc comment restored, metadata-error and
  ensure-guard comments no longer overstate, help text names the trail
  branch (not "the checkpoint") for the picker, resume notices stop
  borrowing status.go's detached-HEAD constant.
